295.title: The shepherd boy's whistle
295.hook: a boy who couldn't read whistles in the synagogue on Yom Kippur, and the Baal Shem says it opened heaven
295.howItsDone: Yom Kippur ends with Neilah, the closing prayer, and then a single long blast of the shofar; some Hasidic teachers tell this story before Neilah to encourage wholehearted prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday you met the Baal Shem Tov and the word hasid. Your line was serve with joy.

Ever been in a room where everyone knew the words except you? A church, a temple, a stadium chant, a family song at a wedding. Everyone's singing, and you're moving your lips, hoping nobody notices. Now a synagogue on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. The room is packed. People have fasted since yesterday. The prayers are long and ancient and all in Hebrew. And in the back sits a village boy who can't read a single word. Hasidim tell this story in many versions.
screen: `EVERYONE KNOWS THE WORDS BUT YOU.` → `YOM KIPPUR, THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` → `A BOY WHO CAN'T READ.`

segments.voice: In one well-known telling, the boy is a shepherd who spends his days in the fields with the flock and has never learned to read. His father brings him to the synagogue of the Baal Shem Tov for Yom Kippur. All day the boy watches everyone pray. He feels it; he wants to pray too. But he has no words. In his pocket is the little whistle he uses in the fields. Near the end of the day, in the closing prayer called Neilah, when the gates of heaven are said to be closing, he can't hold it in. He pulls out the whistle and blows, loud and shrill, right in the middle of the holy silence. People are shocked. His father is mortified. Some want to throw him out. But the Baal Shem Tov finishes the prayer with a shining face, and says: all day our prayers were stuck. They couldn't rise. Then this boy's whistle, which came from the whole of his heart, broke through, and carried all our prayers up with it. The story has no single written source; it's told in different versions, sometimes with a flute, sometimes about another rebbe. But it rests on an old teaching from the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin: the Merciful One wants the heart. What God wants most, the story says, isn't the right words. It's the whole heart, however it comes out.
screen: `A SHEPHERD WHO CAN'T READ.` · `NEILAH: THE GATES ARE CLOSING.` · `THE WHISTLE IN THE SILENCE.` · `GOD WANTS THE HEART.` · then, large: `THE WHISTLE OPENED HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you might have words you use, or none; if you don't, you might still have something you'd want to say to the world, or to life itself. Forget the right words and find your whistle: a sigh, a hum, a thank you, a single honest sentence. Let it come from the whole of you, however plain it is.

Neilah, the closing prayer of Yom Kippur, when the gates of heaven are said to be closing. That's when a shepherd boy blew his whistle, and the Baal Shem Tov said it carried everyone's prayers to heaven.
Your line: the whistle opened heaven. The Merciful One wants the heart. That's day two hundred ninety-five.

296.title: The alphabet prayer
296.hook: a man who knows no prayers recites the alphabet and asks God to arrange the letters
296.tomorrow: the fire, the place, the prayer
296.howItsDone: Before the Amidah, the central standing prayer, Jews quietly say the verse O Lord, open Thou my lips, and many teachers tell the alphabet story to comfort those who don't know the Hebrew prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Neilah, the closing prayer of Yom Kippur, and a shepherd boy whose whistle opened heaven.

You want to write a card to someone who's grieving, and nothing sounds right. You start, delete it, start again. Or you want to apologize, and every sentence comes out wrong. You have the feeling but not the words. Today's Hasidic story is about a man in exactly that spot, standing before God with a full heart and an empty vocabulary. What he did is so simple it almost sounds like a joke. It isn't.
screen: `THE CARD YOU CAN'T WRITE.` → `THE FEELING, BUT NOT THE WORDS.` → `A FULL HEART, NO VOCABULARY.`

segments.voice: The story is told in many ways. In one telling, a simple Jew, a farmer or a villager, is stuck somewhere on the way when it's time to pray, without his prayer book. He never learned the prayers by heart. He only knows the letters. So he stands and says the Hebrew alphabet, slowly, one letter after another. Alef. Bet. Gimel. Dalet. All twenty-two. Then he says something like this: Master of the world, I don't know the prayers. But you know them. Here are all the letters. Please, you arrange them into the right words. In the Hasidic telling, a great rebbe hears of it, or sees it in a vision, and says this was the finest prayer offered that day. Here's what the story sees. Every Hebrew prayer is made from those same letters. Psalms, blessings, the Shema: all of it is alef-bet, arranged. The man isn't skipping the prayer. He's handing over all of it, raw, and trusting the one who hears to put it together. A real line in the daily prayers has the same humility. Before the central standing prayer, Jews say a verse from the Psalms: "O Lord, open Thou my lips." Even the most learned begin by admitting they need help to find the words.

segments.voice: Think of something you want to say, to God if you pray, or to someone in your life, and can't find the words for. Don't hunt for the words now; just set down the raw pieces one by one, like letters: a name, a feeling, a memory. If you pray, you can ask for them to be arranged; if not, simply trust that what's true in them will come through.
Alef-bet, the Hebrew alphabet. A man who knew no prayers said it letter by letter, and asked God to arrange the letters into the right words.
Your line: arrange the letters. Every Hebrew prayer starts out as alef-bet. See you tomorrow.

297.title: The fire, the place, the prayer
297.hook: each generation forgot more of the ritual, but telling the story was enough
297.howItsDone: Telling stories of the rebbes is itself a Hasidic practice, especially at the meal ending Shabbat, and this tale is often told to explain why.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the alef-bet, and a man who handed God every letter and asked for them to be arranged.

Your grandmother made a dish nobody can quite get right anymore. The recipe was in her hands, not on paper. Your mother remembers most of it. You remember some. Your kids may remember only that there was a dish, that it mattered, and the story of the kitchen it came from. Is that a loss? Or is something still carried? Today's Hasidic story is about that kind of forgetting, over four generations of teachers. It's short, and it's a story about stories.
screen: `GRANDMOTHER'S DISH.` → `EACH GENERATION REMEMBERS LESS.` → `A STORY ABOUT STORIES.`

segments.voice: Here's how it's told. When the Baal Shem Tov saw trouble coming for his people, he would go to a certain place in the forest, light a fire, and say a special prayer, and the trouble would be turned away. Years later, when trouble came again, his successor, the Maggid of Mezritch, went to the same place. He said: I don't know how to light the fire. But I can still say the prayer. And it was enough. A generation later, Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sassov went to the forest. I can't light the fire. I don't know the prayer. But I know the place. And it was enough. Then it fell to Rabbi Israel of Ruzhin. He sat in his chair at home, his head in his hands, and said: I can't light the fire. I don't know the prayer. I can't even find the place. All I can do is tell the story. And that has to be enough. And it was. Each generation lost something real, and the story doesn't pretend otherwise. The fire, the prayer, the place: gone, one by one. But the story still carries the thread. The telling keeps a door open. Many people know this tale from the writer Elie Wiesel, who opened one of his novels with it, after enormous loss. And plainly: the sources are late and the versions differ. That seems right for a story about how stories survive.

segments.voice: Hold a story you love, from your family, your faith, your childhood, or from these lessons; if you only remember part of it, hold that part. Who's in it, what happens, and why does it matter to you? Picture telling it to someone, a child, a friend, a partner, so it goes one more generation.
The fire. The Baal Shem Tov's fire, then only the prayer, then only the place, then only the story. And the story was enough.
Your line: the story is enough. Tomorrow, a rebbe afraid of one question. Day two hundred ninety-seven, done.

298.title: Why weren't you Zusya?
298.hook: Reb Zusya feared being asked not why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't Zusya
298.howItsDone: Reb Zusya's question is a widely quoted Hasidic saying, used by rabbis and teachers to encourage people to become fully themselves rather than copies of others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fire, then the prayer, then the place were lost, and the story was enough.

Scroll for thirty seconds and you'll find someone doing your life better. A better parent, a better runner, a better cook, a kinder friend, with better lighting. You can measure yourself against all of them and come up short every time. Now picture an old Hasidic rebbe, much loved, on his deathbed. His students gather around him, and they're surprised to see that he's afraid. He's crying. They ask him why. His answer has been passed from person to person ever since.
screen: `SOMEONE DOING YOUR LIFE BETTER.` → `AN OLD REBBE, AFRAID.` → `WHY ARE YOU CRYING?`

segments.voice: The rebbe is Zusya of Hanipol, an early Hasidic teacher, a student of the Maggid of Mezritch, the Baal Shem Tov's successor. He was known as a humble, joyful, often penniless man, so gentle that people told stories about his kindness. As the story goes, his students tried to comfort him. Rebbe, you've been as faithful as Moses, as kind as Abraham. Surely you have nothing to fear. And Zusya answered, roughly: when I get to the world to come, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? They won't ask, why weren't you Abraham? They'll ask me: Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? And what will I say? That's the whole story, and it turns the usual fear upside down. The worry isn't failing to be someone greater. It's failing to be yourself: not a copy of Moses, but the whole of Zusya, with his own gifts and his own work. In Jewish tradition every person is created in the image of God, and no two people are alike. Zusya takes that seriously. In the story, there's a Zusya-shaped job in the world, and only Zusya can do it. The story is mostly known through modern collections of Hasidic tales, and the exact words differ from teller to teller. But the question has lasted, because it travels so easily.

segments.voice: Let go, for now, of someone you often compare yourself to. Instead, name one thing that's really yours: a kind of humor, a way of listening, something you notice that others miss, a skill your hands have. Picture doing a little more of it, not to impress anyone, just to be a little more you.
Zusya, the Hasidic rebbe who on his deathbed feared not being asked why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't fully himself.
Your line: be Zusya. The question was never about Moses. That's day two hundred ninety-eight.

299.title: Two pockets
299.hook: Rabbi Simcha Bunim: one note says "for my sake the world was made", the other "I am dust and ashes"
299.carry: know which pocket to reach into
299.howItsDone: Many Jews know Rabbi Simcha Bunim's two-pockets teaching, and some literally carry the two sayings on slips of paper as a reminder of balance between dignity and humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zusya, who feared one question more than any other: why weren't you Zusya?

Some days you feel like nothing. A mistake at work, the wrong thing said, and the voice in your head says you don't matter at all. Other days you feel like the center of the universe, and the voice says everyone should notice. Plenty of people swing between the two, sometimes in the same afternoon. A Hasidic rebbe in Poland had a remedy that fits in your clothes. All you need is two pockets, and two slips of paper.
screen: `SOME DAYS: I'M NOTHING.` → `OTHER DAYS: I'M EVERYTHING.` → `TWO POCKETS, TWO SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa lived around 1800. He's remembered as a sharp, honest teacher who hated pretending. The teaching attributed to him goes like this: every person should have two pockets. In one, a note that says: for my sake the world was created. In the other: I am dust and ashes. The wisdom is knowing which pocket to reach into, and when. Both lines are old. You've met the first on this path: it's from the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin. Because the first human being was created alone, each life is a whole world, so every person is obligated to say: for my sake the world was created. The second comes from Genesis. Abraham, bargaining with God to save the city of Sodom, stops himself and says he is "but dust and ashes." Here's the trick. When you're low, feeling worthless, reach into the first pocket: your life is a whole world. When you're puffed up, sure you're owed, reach into the second: you're dust and ashes, and so is everyone else. Neither note alone is the truth. Carry only the first, and you grow arrogant. Carry only the second, and you're crushed. Together they hold you in the middle, where Abraham stood: humble, and bold enough to argue with God.
screen: `TWO POCKETS, TWO NOTES.` · `FOR MY SAKE THE WORLD WAS MADE.` · `I AM BUT DUST AND ASHES.` · `REACH FOR THE ONE YOU NEED.` · then, large: `TWO POCKETS.`

segments.voice: Put one hand on your right side and think: for my sake the world was made; your life is a whole world. Put the other hand on your left and think, gently: I am dust and ashes. Feel both at once, neither one crushing you or lifting you too high; some people even write the two lines on slips of paper and carry them.
Two pockets. One note says for my sake the world was made. The other says I am dust and ashes. Reach for the one you need.
Your line: know which pocket to reach into. Both notes belong to you. Until tomorrow.

300.title: The defense attorney
300.hook: Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev was famous for pleading his people's case before God
300.howItsDone: Stories of Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev are told especially around Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the days of judgment, and Jewish teaching encourages judging others favorably, l'khaf zekhut.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two pockets, one note for when you're low, one for when you're proud. And today is day three hundred: three hundred days on the path.

Some friends always take your side. Call them furious about someone, and they're furious with you. Call them ashamed of yourself, and they say: come on, you were exhausted, anyone would have done that. Sometimes they're too generous. But you always hang up feeling like someone is on your team. Long ago, in the town of Berditchev, in what is now Ukraine, a rebbe played that role for his whole people, in the one courtroom that mattered most to him: before God.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO TAKES YOUR SIDE.` → `ALWAYS ON YOUR TEAM.` → `A REBBE BEFORE GOD.`

segments.voice: His name was Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, a student of the Maggid of Mezritch. People called him the defense attorney of Israel. The Hebrew word is sanegor, an old word borrowed from Greek, meaning an advocate. Pirkei Avot already uses the courtroom picture: every good deed you do gains you an advocate, every wrong gains you an accuser. Levi Yitzchak decided his job was always to be the advocate. There are many stories. Here's one. One morning he saw a wagon driver wrapped in his prayer shawl and tefillin, praying, and at the same time greasing the wheels of his wagon. Anyone else might have scolded him: praying and greasing wheels at once? Levi Yitzchak looked up and said, in effect: Master of the world, look at your people. Even while they grease their wagon wheels, they're praying to you. Same scene, two ways to see it. He always chose the second. He's remembered for arguing with God, too, out loud, on behalf of suffering people, in the line of Moses, who pleaded for Israel after the golden calf. In this tradition, that's read not as disrespect but as a kind of love: taking both God and people seriously enough to argue. The stories come from Hasidic tradition and the details vary. But his reputation is solid: wherever others saw fault, he looked for the defense.

segments.voice: Think of someone you've been judging lately, a coworker, a relative, someone in the news, maybe yourself, and picture them doing the thing that bothers you. Like Levi Yitzchak, look for the defense, the most generous true reading: tired, scared, trying in their clumsy way? If you pray, you can speak up for them in your own words; if not, make their case silently, as well as you can.
Sanegor, the Hebrew word for an advocate. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev always pleaded his people's case before God, and found the good in what others scolded.
Your line: always the defense. Tomorrow, a tailor who argues even harder. Three hundred days, and still walking.

301.title: The tailor's accounting
301.hook: a tailor tells God: I sinned a little, You let children suffer; let us forgive each other
301.howItsDone: Hasidic communities retell stories like the tailor's around Yom Kippur, and many Jews make a cheshbon ha-nefesh, an honest accounting of the soul, in the weeks before the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sanegor, the defense attorney, and Levi Yitzchak, who always looked for his people's defense. Today, the same rebbe meets a tailor who argues even harder.

Yom Kippur in Berditchev, hours into the fast. A crowded synagogue, people tapping their chests as they read the long lists of sins from the prayer book. Among them, the story goes, is a tailor with his own way of doing this. He isn't reciting a list. He's talking to God, quietly, the way you'd talk to a business partner across a kitchen table. Afterward the rebbe, Levi Yitzchak, asks him what he said. The answer is bold. The rebbe's reply is bolder.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR IN BERDITCHEV.` → `A TAILOR WITH HIS OWN WAY.` → `TALKING TO GOD LIKE A PARTNER.`

segments.voice: Here's what the tailor says, as the story is told. Master of the world, I've done wrong. Sometimes I kept the leftover scraps of cloth. Once or twice I ate without washing my hands. Small things. But You have taken babies from their mothers, and mothers from their babies. So let's make an accounting. You forgive me, and I'll forgive You. Let's call it even. Can anyone talk to God like that? Levi Yitzchak doesn't scold him. In the telling, the rebbe's only complaint is that the tailor settled too cheaply. With an argument like that, he says, you could have demanded that God redeem the whole Jewish people. Why isn't this blasphemy? Because it stands in a very old line. Abraham argued with God over Sodom: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" Moses argued. Job argued for chapters. The Hebrew word for an accounting is cheshbon, and the season before Yom Kippur is a time for cheshbon ha-nefesh, an accounting of the soul. The tailor simply turned the ledger both ways. The story doesn't explain why children suffer. Jewish tradition has wrestled with that question at least since Job, whose book never hands him a tidy explanation. This story doesn't pretend to have one. It refuses to fake it. You only argue with someone you believe is listening. And it closes a week of Hasidic tales: the shepherd boy's whistle, the alphabet prayer, the fire and the place, Zusya, two pockets, the defense attorney, and the tailor's accounting.
screen: `I KEPT THE SCRAPS.` · `YOU FORGIVE ME, I FORGIVE YOU.` · `ABRAHAM ARGUED TOO.` · `CHESHBON: AN HONEST ACCOUNTING.` · then, large: `LET'S CALL IT EVEN.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come up that you've been too polite to say, to God if you pray, or to yourself, if that fits you better: a loss that made no sense, a hope that went unanswered, a hurt you keep covering with good manners. You don't have to fix it or explain it. Just say it plainly, inside, the way the tailor did, and let it sit there, said.
Cheshbon, the Hebrew word for an accounting. A Yom Kippur bargain from Berditchev: You forgive me, I forgive You. Honesty, in the one place people expect only apology.
Your line: let's call it even. An honest ledger runs both ways. Day three hundred one, done.

fork.reveal: in the story, Levi Yitzchak says the tailor could have demanded the redemption of the whole people. he pushes the argument further, not back.

original.note: Hebrew: an accounting of the soul, the stock-taking many Jews do before Yom Kippur.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheeky joke about a tailor.
what it means: an honest prayer that says the hard thing out loud, and a rebbe who takes it seriously.
what a scholar hears: the tailor's cheshbon runs in a line back to Abraham at Sodom, and the tale exists in several versions with different rebbes and details.
guess: an accounting, a reckoning of what's owed
a confession recited from a list of sins
a knot tied on the corner of a prayer shawl

sources.ref: Hasidic tale of Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev and the tailor
